title: The SIRMOS mission concept: a space-based near-IR spectroscopic survey of 100 million galaxies in the Euclid Wide Survey footprint
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures, 6 tables, presented at SPIE Space Telescopes and Instrumentation 2026: Optical, Infrared, and Millimeter Wave (August 2026)
summary: SIRMOS is a mission concept for a future NASA Astrophysics Explorer opportunity that aims to revolutionize our understanding of the universe by mapping the large-scale structure of galaxies in unprecedented breadth and detail to explore cosmic origins and evolution. Specifically, the primary science goals of SIRMOS are to discover how cosmic inflation seeded large-scale structure, reveal the nature of the accelerating expansion of the universe, and measure the sum of neutrino masses to exceptionally high precision. Its secondary science goals include determining how environment shapes galaxy evolution at cosmic noon and beyond, and probing the Milky Way's dust-enshrouded regions, reaching the far side of our Galaxy. To accomplish its transformative science goals, SIRMOS executes a 3-year cosmology survey over the Euclid footprint of ~14,000 deg$^2$, obtaining slit spectra for ~100 million galaxies at 1<z<4. SIRMOS is the first space mission designed specifically to leverage Euclid's wide near-infrared (IR) imaging survey for target selection and employs a digital micro-mirror device (DMD) to acquire up to 4,000 simultaneous spectra over a wide 0.9 deg$^2$ field of view. The instrument's excellent spectral resolution of $R=1300$ and continuous wavelength coverage from 1.25--2.5 $\mu$m capture the redshifts of distant galaxies with no gaps, reducing systematic biases to achieve ground-breaking science.

title: A High Precision Metacalibration Response Correction
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures
summary: In Metacalibration the shear response of a weak lensing measurement is estimated by applying an artificial shear to the image, but the shear operation imprints a spin-2 modulation on the image noise power, which biases the measured response. The standard fix adds a sheared noise field that symmetrizes the anisotropy, at the cost of doubling the noise variance ($\sqrt2$ in the noise). The fusion correction presented in this note reaches the same unbiased response while adding only the minimum power needed. It measures the noise power transfer by passing an impulse through the Metacal process, forms the common-level azimuthal deficit that equalizes the spin-2 ($m{=}2$) and spin-6 ($m{=}6$) modulations across the metacal types, and adds just that deficit by filtering the rotated noise field. The fusion correction raises the per-pixel noise by only $\sim2\%$ for a round PSF (versus $\sqrt2$ for the standard correction), rising toward the $\sqrt2$ level only for highly elliptical PSFs.

title: ASTRA: An Autonomous Framework for Physics-Validated Analysis and Hypothesis Generation in Astrophysics
comment: 27 pages - MNRAS - RAS Techniques and Instruments - accepted - in press
summary: We present ASTRA, an autonomous framework for physics-validated analysis and hypothesis generation in astrophysics without per-step human intervention. It integrates dimensional analysis, structural causal models, Bayesian evidence computation, and multi-wavelength data fusion in a single automated workflow. Five test cases on real observational data recover known results: Herschel filament scaling, Chandra Deep Field South cross-matching, SDSS galaxy correlations, Gaia causal inference, and Bayesian virial model selection. A sixth case runs unsupervised on synthetic galaxy data. The main sequence and mass-metallicity relation are recovered, and the outlier detector, with a false-discovery-rate threshold and no contamination parameter, recovers the blind injected fraction on ten sealed datasets (purity > 0.99) and flags nothing on the 3,000-galaxy sample. A knowledge-isolation ablation shows pattern detection and physical validation are invariant to removal of domain knowledge, which affects only interpretation. In a direct comparison, agentic-LLM and pure-ML baselines match the statistical fitting but not the physics-validation stage. They rarely derive the equilibrium benchmark, split evenly on the physical verdict, and adopt a supplied erroneous benchmark in all six trap runs, an astrophysics-specific fine-tuned model completes zero of six runs. On live SDSS DR16 data it flags 197 of 4,999 galaxies at a data-determined threshold, ranked extremes classifiable from withheld spectroscopy. These are recovery validations and capability demonstrations rather than discoveries, with hypothesis generation demonstrated qualitatively.

title: Propulsion Systems for a Starshade Rendezvous Mission with the Habitable World Observatory
comment: 39 pages, 11 figure, 4 tables. Accepted for publication on JATIS
summary: We assess how propulsion and operational constraints affect exo-Earth characterization with a starshade rendezvous mission for a Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO)-like telescope at Sun-Earth L2. Using end-to-end Monte Carlo simulations with EXOSIMS, we model a 60 m starshade for visible-band spectroscopy (500-1000 nm) and a 35 m starshade for near-ultraviolet characterization (250-550 nm). For the 60 m design, we compare AEPS Hall, NEXT ion, and Starlink-class Hall thrusters and examine sensitivity to propellant capacity, the fraction of each retargeting slew spent accelerating and decelerating, and on-orbit refueling. With 1000-3000 kg of initial propellant and no refueling, NEXT provides the highest characterization yield: 9-13% more characterizations than AEPS and 13-16% more than the Starlink-class option. Its higher specific impulse enables more retargeting slews per kilogram of propellant. With refueling, yields converge across thruster choices to about 120 cumulative characterizations over 10 years, while propulsion choice mainly affects the number of refueling events. For the 35 m starshade with AEPS, yields are less sensitive to fuel and are dominated by mission duration and geometric accessibility. Increasing the minimum solar keepout angle from 40 to 50 degrees has little effect on yield; increases from 50 to 65 degrees have a modest effect, while angles above 65 degrees rapidly reduce yield, with severe degradation near 80 degrees. These results distinguish fuel-limited and time- or keepout-limited regimes and guide propulsion selection, tank sizing, refueling policy, and keepout constraints for HWO starshade missions.

title: The Great Chat in the Sky: Aligning Exotic Astronomical Data to Language with AstroBridge
summary: Astronomical observations include images, spectra, and light curves, while the scientific literature describes these objects in natural language. We present AstroBridge, a framework that connects these observations to an LLM through a literature-assisted caption generation pipeline. We used catalog metadata to match observations with scientific texts that describe the same objects. A vision-language model generates descriptive captions from representations of observations, matched passages, and available metadata, creating observation-caption pairs without manual captioning. We train AstroBridge to predict captions directly from raw observations. Modality-specific frozen encoders extract representations that a shared, trainable fusion network aligns with the embedding space of an LLM. In caption-based evaluation of spectra, AstroBridge achieves 91.5% accuracy in distinguishing quasars from galaxies, compared to 69.0% from the base model prior to fine-tuning. Limitations remain in galaxy morphology, classification of minority supernova classes, and the factual quality of generated captions. We believe that AstroBridge's framework is a step towards the goal of aligning the totality of astronomy's diverse, exotic data through the lingua franca of text.

title: Overview And Present Status Of The 4-m International Liquid Mirror Telescope (ILMT)
summary: The International Liquid Mirror Telescope (ILMT) is an inexpensive optical instrument with a diameter of 4 metres, entirely dedicated to astronomical surveys. Its scientific programmes include the detection and study of transients, variable objects, asteroids, comets, low surface brightness galaxies, space debris, etc. The telescope achieved its first light on 29 April 2022 and was officially inaugurated on 21 March 2023. It has been operating regularly since October 2023 and continuously observes the sky passing through the zenith using the SDSS $g^{\prime}$, $r^{\prime}$, and $i^{\prime}$ filters in a narrow band of the sky ($22.3^{\prime}$) centred around the equatorial declination of $+29°21^{\prime}41^{\prime \prime}$. Here we report on the astrometric and photometric performance of the ILMT and summarise the main results obtained since the BINA3 workshop. A great way to raise public awareness is to build a scale model of a liquid mirror telescope. General guidelines for doing so are provided.

title: FLITS: an interactive, reproducible workbench for fast radio burst analysis
comment: 6 pages. Code: this https URL ; documentation: this https URL ; software archive: this https URL
summary: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are brief flashes of radio emission whose time, frequency, and polarization structure constrain their sources and propagation environments. FLITS (Fast-Look Interactive Transient Suite) is an open-source Python package with a browser interface for analysing detected bursts. It combines data inspection, interference mitigation, measurement, and modelling, including fits of the fitburst burst model, in a shared session, and reads SIGPROC filterbank, PSRFITS, and CHIME/FRB HDF5 data. The same routines measure larger samples from the command line and flag bursts whose automatic selections need checking. Trial dispersion measures can be scored by signal-to-noise, by burst structure, or with a smoothed-structure metric that also reports the range of dispersion measures consistent with the best one. Portable session files retain the selected data regions, excluded channels, calibration inputs, available results, input-data checksum, and software provenance, and supported measurements can be replayed from the command line and compared with their saved values. Uncertainty labels identify missing calibration information. A public reference workflow provides downloadable data and numerical checks.

title: Detection and characterisation of Starlink VHF TT&C emissions at 137.055 MHz with the 21 CentiMeter Array
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures, 4tables. Submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Satellite emissions at low frequencies can interfere with astronomical observations. Observations with the EDA2 have revealed recurrent Starlink emissions near 137~MHz, attributed to very high frequency (VHF) telemetry, tracking, and command (TT\&C) transmissions. We aim to characterise Starlink VHF emissions detected with the 21 CentiMeter Array (21CMA) to better assess their potential impact on future low-frequency radio astronomical observations and inform the development of methods to mitigate the resulting interference. We searched five coordinated VHF channels in observations obtained on 15 April 2025 (UTC) and demodulated and decoded candidate signals. Two valid packets are detected at 137.055~MHz, each lasting 1.027584~s and separated by 99.987~s. A blind comparison with 11\,305 active satellites identifies STARLINK-32838 (NORAD ID 62827) as the transmitter, with differential Doppler measurements linking both events to the same spacecraft. Orbital analysis shows that the satellite was undergoing orbit raising and that the limited number of detections was partly attributable to its being below the horizon for most of the observing time. Re-analysis of EDA2 detections indicates that such emissions are not confined to orbit raising. The stronger event's estimated flux density is 9.23~MJy at 1000~km, consistent with previous measurements at the order-of-magnitude level. Signal demodulation and decoding, combined with orbital analysis, can improve the identification and characterisation of satellite-related radio frequency interference. The detection of similar VHF emissions across different orbital phases indicates that their potential interference with low-frequency radio astronomy should not be considered solely in the context of orbit raising.

title: A Point-source Catalogue from Direction-dependent Calibrated 21CMA Images
comment: 22 pages, 19 figures, 7 tables. Accepted for publication in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS)
summary: We present a deep low-frequency radio point-source catalogue centred on the North Celestial Pole (NCP) and extending $5^\circ$ in radius, derived from a single 24-h observation with the 21 CentiMeter Array (21CMA). Covering 75-175 MHz, the catalogue characterises extragalactic foreground point sources for Epoch of Reionization (EoR) studies. Previous 21CMA imaging has been limited by reduced dynamic range caused by direction-dependent effects, particularly the severe grating lobes of ultra-bright sources such as 3C 61.1 and ionospheric phase distortions. Here we apply 21CMAcali, a direction-dependent calibration and imaging pipeline, to mitigate these effects. The angular resolution ranges from 2.3 arcmin at 100 MHz to 1.4 arcmin at 168.75 MHz. The resulting maps show reduced artefacts and background noise, enabling more reliable recovery of faint sources. We construct a catalogue of 1246 radio point sources. Cross-matching with LoTSS-DR3, WENSS, and NVSS enables broad-band spectral fitting, while an independent in-band analysis yields a median spectral index of $\alpha=-0.825$ (where $S \propto \nu^{\alpha}$). The Euclidean-normalised differential source counts at 150 MHz, derived from a dedicated 50-MHz-wide multi-frequency synthesis (MFS) image, are broadly consistent with existing measurements and semi-empirical models at the bright end, whereas the deficit at lower flux densities ($S \lesssim 0.04$ Jy) mainly reflects limited sensitivity and incompleteness. This catalogue improves foreground point-source characterisation in the 21CMA NCP field, demonstrates the value of direction-dependent calibration, and provides a reference for deeper catalogues based on multi-day observations.

title: A Fast and Memory-Efficient Algorithm for Searching Faint Moving Objects using Synthetic Tracking
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures
summary: Detecting unknown faint moving objects using optical imaging is challenging. Long exposure times are infeasible for such targets, as the resulting image streaking causes a loss of signal-to-noise ratio due to energy dispersal across multiple pixels. To address this, synthetic tracking, a track-before-detect method, replaces long exposures with many short exposures, integrating them in post-processing to recover the moving signal. Enabled by modern CMOS detectors with fast readout and low read noise, this technique synthesizes telescope tracking by searching over a grid of velocities. However, the conventional brute-force implementation imposes a significant computational burden: integrating N_f frames of size (N_x,N_y) requires O(N_x N_y N_f^3) operations. This cost becomes prohibitive for megapixel-scale frames with N_f~100. Although dynamic programming can reduce the computational complexity by a factor of N_f, it requires a prohibitive memory of O(N_x N_y N_f^2), unsuitable for large-format detectors. This article presents a novel algorithm to achieve the computational efficiency of dynamic programming while maintaining a memory footprint of just O(N_x N_y N_f) by slightly approximating the computation of frame shifts for alignment. By expressing the shift as a sum of terms proportional to the digits frame index in binary and rounding up each of these terms, frames can be integrated efficiently by hierarchically adding intermediate sums that are shared across different velocities with the same higher bits in binary. The approximation only introduces a small tracking error that increases logarithmically with the number of frames. This advancement enables synthetic tracking to be executed with high energy efficiency, making it practical for deployment on standard workstations rather than requiring high-performance computing infrastructure such as GPU servers or CPU clusters.

title: A Hierarchical Bayesian Differential Calibration of the Gaia DR3 Parallax Zero Point Using Galactic Globular Clusters
summary: Globular clusters (GCs) occupy a broad range of stellar colors and magnitudes while sharing nearly the same distance. Gaia Data Release 3 parallaxes retain systematic zero-point residual variations for GCs, even after the correction by the widely used standard correction model (L21). We derive an empirical residual correction by the Hierarchical Bayesian Model, separating cluster-level offsets from the differential information carried by the member sequences. We first evaluate the L21 baseline at a fixed reference color, which assigns the remaining color-dependent correction to the residual model. Then we model the residual zero point, $\delta Z(G,\nu_{\rm eff})$, with B-splines functions in color and magnitude--color interaction terms. The uncorrected cluster residuals exhibit a negative offset of approximately $25$--$40~\mu{\rm as}$. The L21 baseline removes most of this offset but leaves coherent color- and magnitude-dependent structure. Applying the residual model brings the mean residuals close to zero, especially across most of the sampled color range. In five-fold cross-validation that excludes entire clusters from training, the correction modestly reduces the magnitude- and color-trend RMS relative to the L21 correction. The resulting model therefore provides a differential refinement of the \textit{Gaia} DR3 parallax zero-point within the calibrated domain for GCs, rather than an independent determination of its absolute value.

title: Neglecting Dynamical Microlensing Can Bias Accretion Disk Size Measurements at the Population Level
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables
summary: Microlensing of strongly lensed quasars probes unresolved accretion disks, but many inference methods use static magnification maps with fixed relative microlens positions. Using the GPU-accelerated simulator Microcaustics, we generate ten-year multiband light curves for three quadruply lensed quasar configurations. We compare dynamical microlensing with independent microlens motions against coherent bulk motion, and a microlens mass distribution against equal masses, keeping the velocity distribution of individual microlenses and mean mass fixed. We infer population disk sizes using ridge regression on the means and lower and upper scatters of ten variability and event metrics. We measure biases by applying models trained with simplified physics to simulations including both effects. Models trained on coherent motion interpret the additional variability from evolving caustics as smaller disks. For populations of 128 independent realizations, jointly inferred radii are consistently smaller by 6-28%. Microlens dynamics increase caustic-crossing rates pooled across all four macroimages by 5-15% and r-band high-magnification-event (HME) rates by 13-25%, while shortening median HME durations by 4-12%. Omitting the mass distribution produces configuration-dependent disk-size offsets from -12% to +5%. Including the mass distribution decreases caustic-crossing rates by 6-8% and HME rates by 6-12%. It also narrows the spread of ten-year averaged microlensing time-delay differences between macroimages by a median of 9-12% per system, while microlens dynamics have a smaller, image-pair-dependent effect. These results demonstrate the importance of microlens dynamics for population disk-size inference and motivate simulations that include dynamical microlensing and a microlens mass distribution.

title: The Stellar Populations of Resolved Galaxies
comment: Invited Review. Accepted for publication in Physics Reports. 221 pages (115 main text, 46 appendices, 60 references), 36 figures. Movie of Fig. 7 at this https URL
summary: The study of galaxies outside the Milky Way using observations of resolved stellar populations has experienced extraordinary growth over the past two decades. There now exist panchromatic photometry and precise astrometry for hundreds of millions of individually resolved stars in hundreds of galaxies that span $\sim10^9$ in luminosity, $\sim10^3$ in metallicity, and sample a wide range of environments. Here, we review advances in extragalactic astronomy enabled by resolved stellar population imaging. We summarize major observational programs and focus on four interconnected science areas: the star formation histories of galaxies, 'bursty' star formation, the stellar initial mass function, and the orbital histories of Local Group galaxies. We review the literature in each area, synthesize key findings, identify emerging trends, and discuss how new and future facilities (e.g., JWST, LSST, Euclid, Roman, CSST, ELTs, HWO) will enable further progress. Finally, we highlight shortcomings in current datasets and discuss promising directions for new areas of investigation.

title: Detection of star formation in a near-pristine pocket of the Universe
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, accepted for publication in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
summary: We detect two high-confidence star-forming sources in the environment of a chemically near-pristine ([Fe/H] $<-3.66~;2\sigma)$ Damped Ly$\alpha$ system (DLA) using Keck/KCWI. These are found via the hydrogen Ly$\alpha$ emission line at $\Delta v=-1200$ kms$^{-1}$ (LAE1) and $\Delta v = -200$ kms$^{-1}$ (LAE2) relative to the DLA redshift ($z_{\rm abs} = 3.078$) at an impact parameter of $b=66$ physical kpc and $b=137$ physical kpc. We measure Ly$\alpha$ fluxes of $F(\rm Ly\alpha)_{\rm LAE1} =4.4\pm 0.7\times10^{-18}~\rm erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}$ and $F(\rm Ly\alpha)_{\rm LAE2} =3.8\pm 0.9\times10^{-18}~\rm erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}$. This marks the first detection of star formation in the environment of a chemically near-pristine DLA. We use red channel Keck/KCRM data to place limits on the associated He II 1640 A emission flux of these sources, $F(\rm He\,II)<3.8\times10^{-19}~\rm erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}~(3\sigma)$ and $F(\rm He\,II) <3.7\times10^{-19}~\rm erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}~(3\sigma)$. The weak and narrow properties of the Ly$\alpha$ emission, combined with the inferred position on the mass-metallicity relation, suggest a metal-paucity of these galaxies. Future rest-frame optical observations are required to pin down the metallicity of LAE1 and LAE2 and test if chemically near-pristine DLAs can be used as a signpost to search for primitive, metal-poor galaxies 2 Gyrs after the Big Bang.

title: What sets the star-formation rate in the Milky Way? I. A multi-scale view of the star-formation rate
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, submitted to A&A
summary: Context. The star-formation rate (SFR) is one of the key quantities that characterizes the star formation process and has been extensively investigated both observationally and theoretically. Aims. We aim to provide a coherent multi-scale view of star formation by connecting Galactic-scale conditions (kpc) to the properties of individual star-forming clumps at sub-parsec scales. Methods. We perform a set of numerical simulations with large-scale turbulent forcing designed to reproduce physical conditions typical of the solar neighbourhood. Using adaptive zooming down to 0.03 pc, we obtain a population of star-forming clumps that is analyzed and compared with observational catalogues in a companion paper. Results. For column densities and velocity dispersions consistent with Galactic values, the resulting SFR is close to the rate inferred for the Milky Way. Comparing this value with the SFR expected from pure free-fall collapse shows that turbulence provides multiscale support that lowers the SFR by more than an order of magnitude. Additional regulation by stellar feedback, including ionizing radiation and protostellar outflows, likely reduces the SFR by an additional factor of 3-10. Comparisons with observations across multiple spatial scales show good overall agreement with this model. Conclusions. These results support a picture in which turbulence plays a central role in regulating star formation in the Milky Way. In combination with stellar feedback, it limits the star formation efficiency to only a few percent. Key words. stars: formation -- ISM: clouds -- physical processes: turbulence

title: Dependence of Merger-driven Star Formation and Gas-phase Metallicity Evolution on Merger Type and Stellar Mass
comment: 24 pages, 10 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Galaxy mergers play a fundamental role in driving gas inflows, altering star formation, and redistributing metals, yet how these processes depend on merger type, merger stage, and progenitor galaxy properties remains incompletely understood. In this work, we investigate the resolved impact of mergers on star formation rate (SFR) and gas-phase metallicity using MaNGA integral-field spectroscopy and the MaNGA Galaxy Merger Catalog of Comerford et al. (2024). By comparing merger galaxies to matched controls, we quantify local offsets in SFR and metallicity as functions of merger type, merger stage, stellar mass, and galactocentric radius. We find that major mergers generally exhibit stronger SFR enhancement and greater metallicity dilution than minor mergers. In major mergers, SFR enhancement is often spatially extended, whereas in minor mergers it is weaker and more centrally concentrated. The SFR response in major mergers varies non-monotonically with merger stage, with stronger enhancement in the early (first-passage) and post-coalescence stages and weaker enhancement in the late (between-passage) stage. Metallicity dilution is generally strongest in early-stage major mergers and weaker at later stages, although this stage dependence is not monotonic across all stellar-mass bins. We also find stellar-mass dependence that lower-mass systems show stronger metallicity dilution in both major and minor mergers, while the strongest SFR enhancement occurs in intermediate- and high-mass major mergers. These results show that the resolved star formation and metallicity responses depend jointly on merger type, merger stage, and stellar mass and exhibit different behaviors across the merger sequence.

title: Prospects for Near-Far Constraints on Reionization from Simulated LSST Observations of Milky Way Dwarf Galaxies and Stellar Streams
comment: 31 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables, submitted to ApJ. Data available at this http URL
summary: The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will detect resolved stellar populations of intact dwarf galaxies and disrupted stellar streams in the Milky Way (MW) halo and beyond, opening a new avenue for near-field cosmology, particularly for constraining the faint galaxies during reionization. To interpret these data, we present and publicly release mock LSST catalogs of satellites, stellar streams, phase-mixed galaxies, and field galaxies around 13 MW-mass hosts in the FIRE-2 zoom-in simulations, generated with \textsf{py-ananke}. Using a surface brightness limit of $\mu_{g} \leq 34$ $\rm{mag}$ $\rm{arcsec^{-2}}$, we find that $\approx29\%$ of streams with $M_{\star} \gtrsim 5 \times 10^5$ $M_{\odot}$ are detectable with tidal tails, while another $\approx38\%$ are detectable only through their bound progenitors and would appear as satellites. We estimate that $\approx96\%$ of satellites and $\approx64\%$ of field galaxies (out to $\sim$3.5 Mpc) with $M_{\star} \gtrsim 10^{5}$ $M_{\odot}$ are detectable, decreasing to $\approx$59\% and $\approx$42\% for $M_{\star} \gtrsim 10^{4.5}$ $M_{\odot}$ owing to resolution limits. Including streams detectable as satellites reproduces the radial distribution of observed MW satellites, suggesting that some observed satellites may be bound remnants of disrupted systems. Our mock galaxies match the sizes of observed satellites with $M_{\rm{V}} \lesssim -6$. Star-formation histories computed from only the detectable stars broadly recover the simulated star-formation histories. As an application, we test the near-far technique for reconstructing the proto-MW ultraviolet luminosity function (UVLF) during reionization ($z \gtrsim 6$). Adding the detectable streams improves the recovered faint-end slope at $z = 7$ and reduces the halo-to-halo scatter by $\approx33\%$.

title: What sets the star-formation rate in the Milky Way?. II. Comparing the star-forming clumps from simulations and observations
comment: 16 pages, 10 figures, 5 tables, 4 appendices. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Context. Linking the star formation (SF) properties of dense clumps to their parent large-scale environment is a key step to interpret Galactic surveys. Achieving a consistent, multi-scale picture of SF requires a comparative analysis of observations and simulations. Aims. We exploit kiloparsec-scale magneto-hydrodynamic simulations designed to reproduce local Milky Way conditions. Leveraging the wide range of scales covered by the simulations (reaching a resolution of 0.03 pc), we aim to compare the properties of the simulated population of star-forming clumps with observational catalogues. Methods. After extracting the star-forming structures with the HOP clump-finding algorithm, we compare their physical (mass and size) and SF properties (SF rate and efficiency) with those of the Hi-GAL compact source catalogue. Results. Despite the different methodologies and the three-dimensional nature of our clump extraction, the simulated clumps show good agreement with the observed sample in their mass and size distributions. We discover a consistently linear relation between mass and SF rate (SFR) for the simulated clumps, which is remarkably independent of the initial conditions of the boxes. Using scaling relations to distinguish between turbulence- and gravity-regulated gas inflow onto the clump scales, we find tentative evidence in favour of a gravity-regulated regime of SF at the probed sub-parsec scales. Key words. methods: numerical - stars: formation - ISM: clouds

title: The Cosmic Ultraviolet Baryon Survey X: Density and Pressure Profiles of Clumpy Circumgalactic Gas at $z=0.4-0.7$
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal after minor revisions. 24 pages with 8 figures, and a 27-page appendix with 23 additional figures
summary: The thermodynamic state and turbulent properties of the cool circumgalactic medium (CGM) are investigated for 23 galaxies and galaxy groups at intermediate redshift ($z=0.4$--0.7) in the Cosmic Ultraviolet Baryon Survey (CUBS) midz sample using background QSOs within the virial radius. Kinematically resolved absorption-line measurements from Hubble Space Telescope/COS and STIS spectra, combined with photoionization modeling, yield gas densities of $n_\mathrm{H}\approx10^{-4}$--$10^{-2} \ \mathrm{cm}^{-3}$, temperatures of $T\approx(1$--$5) \times 10^4\,\mathrm{K}$, and non-thermal line broadening of $b_\mathrm{NT}\approx2$--$30 \ \mathrm{km \ s^{-1}}$ for individual cool clumps. Combined with published samples at similar redshifts, the results indicate that photoionization equilibrium accurately describes the cool CGM and that turbulent motions are predominantly subsonic. At fixed projected distance, cool-gas density decreases systematically with halo mass, while inferred cool-gas pressures in $M_h\approx10^{12}$--$10^{13}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ halos are consistent with hot-gas pressures inferred from stacked X-ray observations. The analysis uncovers a near constant total cool gas mass across a broad halo mass range, which directly translates to a declining baryon mass fraction in the cool phase from $\approx 6$--$19\%$ in halos of $M_h \approx 10^{12}\, \mathrm{M}_\odot$ to $\approx 0.6$--$1.5\%$ in halos of $M_h \approx 10^{13}\, \mathrm{M}_\odot$. Finally, several CUBS galaxies exhibit kinematically aligned low- and high-ionization species spanning up to two orders of magnitude in density, reflecting local fluctuations in the halo gas pressure.

title: Heavy Seeds and the Multi-scale Fueling of Early Supermassive Black Holes and Little Red Dots
comment: 20 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to ApJ
summary: The formation of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) in the early Universe has been a longstanding mystery due to the brief period available to assemble them. More recently, the unexpected discovery with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) of Little Red Dots (LRDs), compact sources exhibiting signatures of active galactic nuclei (AGN), has accentuated this challenge. Cosmological simulations investigating their formation and evolution confront the limitation that the compact scale of SMBH/LRD physics cannot be simultaneously resolved with the larger-scale cosmological environment. We address this limitation by utilizing a cutout technique, selecting a targeted region around an SMBH seed from a cosmological parent simulation and re-running the cutout at higher (sub-pc) resolution for shorter periods. We explore two SMBH formation scenarios: the standard, light seed stellar-remnant case, and the heavy-seed, direct collapse black hole (DCBH) channel. Within the high-resolution achieved by the cutouts, the DCBH, due to its larger mass, is able to induce a buildup of high density gas nearby and accrete gas in bursts of super-Eddington phases, growing in mass and producing an LRD-like spectrum. In contrast, the stellar remnant cannot do so and remains dormant, unable to affect the nearby gas or significantly evolve by gas accretion alone. Therefore, we find that observed high-redshift SMBHs and LRDs require the existence of heavy seeds to assemble dense gas around themselves, enabling efficient growth and producing red optical spectra with strong Balmer breaks resembling LRDs.

title: Protostellar Outflows at the EarliesT Stages (POETS) X. Preliminary statistics of 6.7 GHz masers near POETS sources
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures
summary: So far, the POETS survey has focused on studying at high angular resolution the properties of both 22.2 GHz H2O masers and the radio continuum emission near young stellar objects (YSOs). Now, we want to add the information coming from another star formation tracer, the Class II 6.7 GHz CH3OH (methanol) maser, towards the same POETS targets. We seek to probe the existence of 6.7 GHz maser emission near POETS sources with high sensitivity observations and study their kinematic properties with respect to local radio continuum and 22.2 GHz maser emission at high angular and spectral resolutions. Within the POETS survey, we used the Very Large Array (VLA) in the A configuration, operating at high spectral resolution (0.1 km/s) and achieving a sensitivity of a few mJy/beam per channel map, in order to (i) probe the emission from methanol gas in the 6.7 GHz maser transition and (ii) trace its absolute spatial distribution and local standard of rest velocity. We present a preliminary analysis of 6.7 GHz CH3OH maser emission toward a subsample of the POETS survey (22 fields observed so far), 60 % of which show detection above a brightness temperature threshold of 10^7 K. Five sources among this subsample are new detections. We draw a 6.7 GHz maser brightness function by studying the distribution of the intrinsic luminosity of the maser population and predict that more than 30 % of the whole population is undetected at typical interferometric sensitivities of a few 10 mJy/beam. We confirm that 6.7 GHz masers arise close to the young star they are associated with and quantify that, on average, 90 % of them are distributed within radii of 3000 au only. Furthermore, we find a tight correlation between the 6.7 GHz maser luminosity coming from a given source and the local free-free emission, suggesting that the radio continuum provides the dominant source of seed photons amplified by the methanol gas.

title: The inner galaxy as a window on its early assembly: lessons from a cosmological Milky Way analogue
comment: 19 pages, 14 figures, 1 table, submitted to MNRAS
summary: Characterising the assembly history of the inner Milky Way is a key goal of upcoming spectroscopic surveys, yet disentangling its overlapping stellar components remains challenging. We investigate the chemodynamics of the centre of a Milky Way analogue in the Auriga Superstars cosmological hydrodynamical simulation suite, focusing on a high-resolution halo (~ 800 M_sun star particles) with a realistic galactic bar and accretion history. We classify stars within the inner 4 kpc into proto-galaxy, subsequent in-situ, and accreted components to assess their distinguishability using kinematics, dynamics, ages, and metallicities. Stellar net rotation declines sharply between [Fe/H]=0 and [Fe/H]=-1, marking the transition from disc-like in-situ stars to the proto-galaxy. While significant chemical and dynamical overlaps complicate the search for structures in energy-angular momentum (E-Lz) space, metal-poor stars ([Fe/H]<-1) at low energy form a remarkably pure (>97%) sample of proto-galaxy stars. Conversely, the high-energy, metal-poor tail offers the best chance of detecting accreted debris. However, at high energies the inner accreted halo is dominated by low-mass systems (M_star ~ 10^7 - 10^9 M _sun), not the earliest massive mergers. Dynamically, few clues remain from early mergers, and early enrichment is rapid and similar across progenitors. In-situ contamination is an issue for [Fe/H]>-1 throughout E-Lz space. Overall, while accurate stellar ages and high-precision chemical abundances may help further constrain the Milky Way's history, we should be cautious when associating stars with individual merger events in the inner galaxy.

title: Unveiling the nonthermal environments of NGC 3411 and NGC 5903 through new MeerKAT observations
summary: Galaxy groups are key laboratories for investigating the interplay between active galactic nucleus (AGN) outbursts and the dynamical processes of the intra-group medium. We aim to characterize the morphology, spectral properties, and magnetic field structure of the diffuse nonthermal radio emission in two peculiar galaxy groups, NGC 3411 and NGC 5903, selected from an originally larger sample, in order to constrain its origin and its connection with the dynamics of the intra-group medium. We present new MeerKAT UHF- and L-band observations of the two groups, complemented by archival Chandra and XMM-Newton data already analyzed in previous works. In NGC 3411, we detect extended radio emission surrounding the central AGN over scales of ~70 kpc, and resolve previously undetected arc-shaped substructures on scales of ~20-30 kpc. This extended component exhibits a relatively uniform steep spectrum ($\alpha$ ~ -1.7). We discuss possible scenarios for its origin, including mini-halos, aged AGN plasma, weak shocks, and the possibility of a radio galaxy observed along the line of sight. In NGC 5903, MeerKAT reveals a complex filamentary morphology, including a previously unknown ring-like structure surrounding the central AGN. Spectral-index mapping shows localized flattening ($\alpha$ ~ -0.9) along the north arc, while polarization data reveal ordered magnetic fields and a patchy rotation measure distribution across the source. Together with the disturbed X-ray morphology, these results support a scenario in which fossil AGN plasma has been redistributed and locally reenergized by group-scale dynamical processes such as turbulence, shear, and weak compression. Our results demonstrate that galaxy groups can host a rich variety of nonthermal phenomena, whose properties can only be fully revealed through the combination of sensitive, high-resolution, and multifrequency radio observations.

title: NOCTURNE. VI. Hour-timescale radio variability in early-stage active galactic nucleus SDSS J122844.81+501751.2
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, submitted to A&A
summary: Recently, a sample of radio-weak active galactic nuclei (AGN) was discovered to exhibit extreme Jy-level radio flares at 37~GHz. The origin of these extraordinary flares remains unknown. All sources host low-mass supermassive black holes, and most of them can be classified as narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. We employed multiwavelength observations to investigate one of these sources, SDSS J122844.81+501751.2, during a period of high 37~GHz activity. Our data include radio observations from Metsähovi Radio Observatory (MRO) at 37~GHz, OVRO at 15~GHz, and JVLA at 15, 22, and 33~GHz, as well as optical, UV, and X-ray observations from \textit{Swift}/XRT and UVOT. We studied the variability of the multiwavelength light curves (LC) using statistical tests, as well as derived the $e$-folding timescales of the flares. Utilising the timescales and the observed flare properties, we estimated the variability brightness temperatures and Doppler factors associated with the flares. Most individual LCs do not show statistically significant variability, which is likely due to the low number of measurements. The shortest timescale we estimated is only 1.1~hours, measured between MRO 37~GHz and JVLA 33~GHz detections. This is the fastest intrinsic radio variability reported in an AGN so far. This yielded an extreme variability brightness temperature of $T_\mathrm{B}$ = 4.20 $~\times$ 10$^{18}$~K and a variability Doppler factor of 438. We discuss magnetic eruptions near the black hole as a possible explanation for the extreme radio flares, and show that both incoherent and coherent processes can produce flares at these timescales. These flares challenge our current understanding of AGN radio variability. Whereas magnetic eruptions offer a viable explanation for the flares, more observations, preferably broadband and including polarisation, will be required to confirm their origin. (abridged)

title: Impact of Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus Debris on Milky Way Escape-velocity Estimates in TNG50
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures, accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: The escape velocity is a key probe of the Milky Way (MW) potential, but standard estimates can be biased by unrelaxed substructures. Using MW analogs from the TNG50 cosmological simulation, we investigate the impact of the dominant, highly radial Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus (GSE) debris on escape-velocity measurements. We introduce an adaptive selection strategy that balances statistical reliability with sample size to identify the power-law decline regime of the local halo velocity distribution. Applying this strategy to 16 MW analogs with prominent GSE-like structures and continuous high-velocity tails, we find that retaining GSE-like stars yields a systematic underestimate, with a recovery fraction of $97.5^{+2.1}_{-2.9}\%$, while removing GSE-like stars alone increases the recovery fraction to $99.4^{+2.1}_{-2.5}\%$. The $\sim 2\%$ underestimation of the escape velocity corresponds to an $\sim 6\%$ underestimation of the total mass. This improvement persists in LAMOST-like magnitude and footprint selection. GSE-like debris is therefore a key contributor to the systematic underestimation of escape-velocity measurements, with direct implications for the inferred MW mass.

title: ASKAP Discovery of a Giant Odd Radio Circle at $z=0.15$
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables
summary: Odd radio circles (ORCs) are a recently recognized class of faint, roughly circular diffuse radio sources, typically a few hundred kiloparsecs across, whose origin is still debated. We report the serendipitous discovery of a giant ORC, ORC~J1928$-$5056, in 856~MHz continuum data from the ASKAP observations. The emission forms a single, mildly elliptical structure $4^{\prime}$ across, corresponding to $0.63$~Mpc at the redshift $z=0.1507$ of the central galaxy LEDA~140850, the brightest cluster galaxy of Abell~3639, which makes it one of the largest single ORCs known. After subtracting the radio nucleus associated with the host galaxy, the ORC has a flux density of 73~mJy integrated within an area of $\sim 12$~arcmin$^2$, i.e.\ a mean surface brightness of only $1.7$~$\mu$Jy~arcsec$^{-2}$, and a rest-frame luminosity of $L_{1.4}=2\times10^{24}$~W~Hz$^{-1}$, comparable to those of the most luminous ORCs. Including its nucleus, the system reaches $L_{1.4}=6.6\times10^{24}$~W~Hz$^{-1}$, higher than that of any other ORC reported so far. The host is a massive ($M_{\ast}\sim10^{11}\,M_{\odot}$), passive elliptical galaxy with negligible star formation. It contains an AGN jet with a power-law spectrum of index $\alpha=-0.877\pm0.089$ between 856 and 1656~MHz. Finally, we discuss the implications for ORC formation models and the observations needed to establish the nature of this system.

title: A Hierarchical Bayesian Differential Calibration of the Gaia DR3 Parallax Zero Point Using Galactic Globular Clusters
summary: Globular clusters (GCs) occupy a broad range of stellar colors and magnitudes while sharing nearly the same distance. Gaia Data Release 3 parallaxes retain systematic zero-point residual variations for GCs, even after the correction by the widely used standard correction model (L21). We derive an empirical residual correction by the Hierarchical Bayesian Model, separating cluster-level offsets from the differential information carried by the member sequences. We first evaluate the L21 baseline at a fixed reference color, which assigns the remaining color-dependent correction to the residual model. Then we model the residual zero point, $\delta Z(G,\nu_{\rm eff})$, with B-splines functions in color and magnitude--color interaction terms. The uncorrected cluster residuals exhibit a negative offset of approximately $25$--$40~\mu{\rm as}$. The L21 baseline removes most of this offset but leaves coherent color- and magnitude-dependent structure. Applying the residual model brings the mean residuals close to zero, especially across most of the sampled color range. In five-fold cross-validation that excludes entire clusters from training, the correction modestly reduces the magnitude- and color-trend RMS relative to the L21 correction. The resulting model therefore provides a differential refinement of the \textit{Gaia} DR3 parallax zero-point within the calibrated domain for GCs, rather than an independent determination of its absolute value.

title: A Collimated Protostellar Outflow Likely Driven by Jet and Reshaped by Environment in the Sagittarius C Cloud of the Central Molecular Zone
comment: Submitted to ApJ
summary: The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) at the center of the Galaxy provides a nearby laboratory for studying star formation under extreme physical and chemical conditions. Recent ALMA (Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array) observations have identified 43 candidate protostellar outflows in three CMZ clouds. One of these, the Sgr C-F#2 outflow in Sagittarius C (Sgr C), has a highly collimated lobe extending approximately 0.8 pc in projection. Here we present a joint analysis of ALMA observations of SiO J=8-7, 5-4, and 2-1. We use local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) and non-LTE methods to constrain the SiO column densities, H2 number density, and gas temperature. The low SiO rotational temperatures and higher kinetic temperatures inferred from non-LTE methods suggest subthermal excitation. The elongated SiO morphology, shock-excited gas, position-velocity structure, and the alignment of the red shifted molecular lobe with JWST infrared knots altogether favor jet-dominated entrainment, whereas a broader disk-wind component close to the source cannot be excluded. The outflow shows asymmetries in its morphology and physical properties, which can be attributed to dense gas on the path of its lobe impeding its propagation and feedback from a nearby HII region imposing different pressure on its two sides.

title: Excitation and Destruction of Small Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons by the Luminous Seyfert Nucleus of NGC 4151
comment: 17 pages, 10 figures, submitted to ApJ
summary: We present a spatially-resolved detection of $3.3\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ emission from polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) within the circumnuclear ${\sim}200\,\mathrm{pc}$ of the archetypal Seyfert galaxy NGC 4151, using new JWST NIRSpec/IFU spectroscopy. PAHs are detected down to the innermost $50\,\mathrm{pc}$, though it is likely that PAHs also exist at smaller radii, as PAH detections closer than this seem to be limited by continuum dilution. This is contrary to expectations that PAH grains, especially the smallest grains that carry the $3.3\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ feature, could not survive near an active galactic nucleus (AGN). Furthermore, the surface brightness of PAH emission increases as radius from the nucleus decreases. We interpret this as evidence that the AGN supplies energy for PAH excitation by driving ultraviolet emission in nearby H and $\mathrm{H_2}$ gas. We do not detect PAH emission within the narrow line region (NLR) that hosts highly ionized and outflowing gas, suggesting that the AGN may also destroy PAHs in these regions, depending on geometry. Together, these results show that an AGN has a complex, multifaceted role in the life cycle of PAHs and in PAH excitation.

title: Topological Centrality in Gaia Open Clusters
summary: Open clusters exhibit diverse spatial structures that provide insight into their formation and dynamical evolution. We investigate the relationship between stellar mass segregation, network topology, and dynamical age in 871 dynamically unevolved open clusters ($\tau = t/t_{\rm rh} \leq 1$) from Gaia-based catalogs. We construct three-dimensional k-nearest-neighbor graphs and measure Degree Centrality (DC), Closeness Centrality (CL), and Betweenness Centrality (BC). For each measure, we define a network-based mass segregation ratio (MSR) by comparing the mean centrality of the most massive stars with that of all cluster members. We test the stability of these measures across connectivity parameters $k=5$--20 and compare them with the classical 3D MSR, $\Lambda_{\rm MSR,3D}$, and dynamical age. All three network ratios show positive correlations with $\Lambda_{\rm MSR,3D}$, strongest for closeness centrality, while their correlations with dynamical age are weak. These results demonstrate that network analysis provides a complementary approach to studying stellar structure and mass segregation in open clusters.

title: Rare Blue-core BCGs as Optical Signatures of ICM Cooling
comment: Submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Blue cores in brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) trace recent central activity associated with cooling cluster atmospheres. We search for blue cores at $z<0.6$ in five eROSITA all-sky surveys using X-ray data, optical imaging, and optical spectroscopy. We identify 379 blue-core BCGs among 11352 systems (3.3%), although contamination increases toward higher redshift. Of these, 98 (0.86%) are X-ray bright. Their defining signature is a central $g-r$ color at least 0.2 mag bluer than the reference population within $a=20$ kpc before returning to the normal BCG envelope. Ha emission equivalent width correlates strongly with the blue continuum excess, consistent with young stellar components comprising ~0.1-1% of pre-existing stellar mass. Line ratios indicate widespread LINER-like excitation, with a larger star-forming contribution in blue Ha emitters but substantial non-stellar excitation. This activity is closely linked to the thermodynamics of the host-cluster gas. At $0.1R_{500}$, cooling times decrease from BCGs without significant Ha emission to red and then blue Ha emitters. Blue BCGs preferentially occur in clusters with $L_{\rm X,300}>10^{44}$ erg s$^{-1}$; red Ha emitters also favor higher X-ray luminosities. The blue-core fraction rises with optical richness. For systems with $t_{\rm cool}(0.1R_{500})<20$ Gyr, doubling richness increases the odds of hosting a blue-core BCG by $2.45\pm0.39$. This indicates that cluster scale carries information beyond cooling time, plausibly through the amount of gas available for cooling and condensation. The scarcity of blue BCGs without significant Ha emission disfavors isolated short bursts followed by long Ha-quiet fading phases. It can instead be explained by sustained or closely recurrent star formation over timescales much longer than 100 Myr, or by Ha persisting through additional excitation mechanisms as the young stellar component fades.

title: Simulations agree: the Milky Way's satellites are disrupting
comment: 6+3 pages, 3+1 figures. Submitted to MNRAS Letters, comments are welcome
summary: Recent analyses of simulated Milky Way-mass galaxies have highlighted the prevalence of satellites undergoing tidal disruption. However, these have focused on single hydrodynamical codes with a number of limitations, making it unclear how generic this result is. We compare satellite disruption in four models: two cosmological hydrodynamical simulations (Auriga and FIRE), cosmological $N$-body simulations with stellar particle tagging (Aquarius), and a semi-analytic model with varying host disk properties (SatGen). For all systems, we compute the fraction of stellar mass retained by the progenitor ($f_\text{bound}$) at the present day. We find a remarkable agreement between FIRE, Aquarius, and SatGen; all predict that $\sim$20 to 30 per cent of classical-mass satellites have $f_\text{bound} < 0.9$ ($\sim$5 to 10 per cent have $f_\text{bound} < 0.5$). Satellites in Auriga experience substantially more mass loss than other simulations, which we attribute to their massive central galaxies and large satellite sizes prior to infall. In the ultra-faint regime captured by Aquarius and SatGen, disruption rates are comparable to or exceeding those for classical satellites. The ubiquity of mass loss across models presents both an exciting opportunity (a plethora of stellar streams awaiting discovery) and a nuisance (for theorists using satellite counts to constrain dark matter).

title: A Large Diversity in the Quiescent Fractions of Massive Galaxies in Proto-clusters at $z\sim4-6$ in the FRESCO GOODS fields
comment: Submitted to ApJ. 21 pages, 11 figures, 5 tables
summary: To constrain the emergence of the first quiescent galaxies (QGs) and their connection to large-scale structure, we search for rare, high-redshift QGs in proto-clusters using spectral energy distribution modeling, multiple rest-frame color diagnostics, and visual inspection. Our sample includes 12 QG candidates with stellar masses log(M*/Msun) ~ 9-11 in four proto-clusters at z ~ 4-6 within GOODS-North (GOODS-N) and GOODS-South (GOODS-S). The selection uses 11 NIRCam filters in GOODS-N and 17 NIRCam plus 2 MIRI filters in GOODS-S, combined with 9 ancillary HST filters, covering 0.4-7.7 microns. We measure an increasing quiescent fraction with stellar mass, with averages of 1.0%(+0.7/-0.4; 5/502), 3.5%(+2.8/-1.7; 4/115), and 33.3%(+22.2/-17.5; 3/9) for log(M*/Msun) = 9 - 9.75, 9.75 - 10.5, 10.5 - 11.25, respectively, across four proto-clusters. Notably, the two GOODS-N proto-clusters at z=4.406 and z=5.194 have a quiescent fraction of 100% (2/2 at z=4.406; 1/1 at z=5.194) in their highest mass bin (log(M*/Msun) > 10.5), whereas the proto-clusters in GOODS-S at similar redshifts have zero massive quiescent galaxies. Contrary to the expectation that massive galaxies occupy cluster centers at z~0, our QGs are found primarily on the outskirts of overdensity peaks. We also find fewer robust QGs at z>5 (1/8) and none in the z=5.384 proto-cluster, consistent with simulations suggesting that efficient quenching mechanisms had not yet matured. Our results highlight the pronounced variations in quiescent fractions across proto-clusters at z>4. The emerging diversity of proto-cluster QG populations calls for a stronger understanding of the role of environment in early galaxy evolution.

title: The CGM in a New Light: Emitted H$α$, [NII], and [OIII] around Simulated Dwarf Galaxies
comment: 22 pages, 14 figures
summary: Mapping the circumgalactic medium (CGM) in emission is a critical next step in understanding its role in the baryon cycle and galaxy evolution, and dwarf galaxies ($M_{\star}\lesssim 10^9 M_{\odot}$) are essential laboratories to study the effects of feedback on the CGM. Using the Marvelous Massive Dwarfs simulation suite, we model the CGM surface brightness (SB) around dwarf galaxies in H$\alpha$, [NII]$\lambda$6583, and [OIII]$\lambda$5007, lines accessible to current integral-field spectrographs (e.g., MUSE and KCWI) and to narrow-band imaging with the MOTHRA telephoto array. We investigate trends in SB magnitude, extent, and geometry as well as correlations with gas kinematics, recent star formation, and galaxy size. Emission in the three lines typically traces distinct CGM structures and phases. SB and the size of the emitting region can differ significantly at a given galaxy mass, but enhancements or suppression in either brightness or extent correlate well across lines. Typically, emission is preferentially eccentric and oriented along the galaxy's semi-minor axis. While outflows are key drivers in dispersing metals into the CGM and shaping SB, they remain difficult to identify in SB maps and contribute $\sim40\%$ of the total SB across lines and galaxy masses, while inflows contribute $\sim50\%$. Finally, we identify evidence for a positive correlation between SB and recent star formation and weaker but still significant evidence for a negative correlation between SB and HI disk size. These results link CGM emission to both a galaxy's recent star formation and its cumulative evolution, yielding predictions that ongoing surveys can test and further establishing emission mapping as a new window into the baryon cycle.

title: How common are extreme scattering events?: First large sample from the ASKAP VAST survey
comment: Under review in The Astrophysical Journal, any comments are welcome
summary: Compact radio sources are occasionally observed to undergo extreme scattering events (ESEs): large, chromatic flux-density variations, often by more than a factor of two, over a few months. These were interpreted to be a smooth plasma lensing phenomenon due to AU-scale structures in the ISM. Although ESEs were discovered decades ago, observationally, only a few tens of ESEs have been reported, often from individual sources monitored at very high cadences. As such, the nature of the plasma lenses generating such events remains elusive. In this article, we present the most comprehensive sample of ESEs to date, using the ASKAP Variables and Slow Transients (VAST) survey. We report the discovery of a three-tier sample --- 72 sources that show promising ESE events (gold), 76 sources that are likely ESE-exhibiting (silver), and an additional 88 sources where ESE events are one plausible explanation (bronze). We show that the light curves demonstrate varied morphologies, which can be interpreted in terms of the source size and the strength of the lens in the paradigm of a simple one-dimensional Gaussian lens model. The spatial distribution of ESEs shows an appreciable excess in the direction of the Galactic center and along the Galactic loops. Using this sample, we infer an overall rate of 0.012 such events per year per deg^2 (or 0.006 events per source per year) for our (gold+silver) sample, for sources with mean flux density above 5 mJy at 888 MHz (0.01% of all isolated point sources detected in VAST).

title: Neglecting Dynamical Microlensing Can Bias Accretion Disk Size Measurements at the Population Level
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables
summary: Microlensing of strongly lensed quasars probes unresolved accretion disks, but many inference methods use static magnification maps with fixed relative microlens positions. Using the GPU-accelerated simulator Microcaustics, we generate ten-year multiband light curves for three quadruply lensed quasar configurations. We compare dynamical microlensing with independent microlens motions against coherent bulk motion, and a microlens mass distribution against equal masses, keeping the velocity distribution of individual microlenses and mean mass fixed. We infer population disk sizes using ridge regression on the means and lower and upper scatters of ten variability and event metrics. We measure biases by applying models trained with simplified physics to simulations including both effects. Models trained on coherent motion interpret the additional variability from evolving caustics as smaller disks. For populations of 128 independent realizations, jointly inferred radii are consistently smaller by 6-28%. Microlens dynamics increase caustic-crossing rates pooled across all four macroimages by 5-15% and r-band high-magnification-event (HME) rates by 13-25%, while shortening median HME durations by 4-12%. Omitting the mass distribution produces configuration-dependent disk-size offsets from -12% to +5%. Including the mass distribution decreases caustic-crossing rates by 6-8% and HME rates by 6-12%. It also narrows the spread of ten-year averaged microlensing time-delay differences between macroimages by a median of 9-12% per system, while microlens dynamics have a smaller, image-pair-dependent effect. These results demonstrate the importance of microlens dynamics for population disk-size inference and motivate simulations that include dynamical microlensing and a microlens mass distribution.

title: Variable Stars in Local Group Galaxies IX: Tracing the Complex History of NGC 205
summary: We present the most extensive catalogue of variable stars in NGC 205 to date, based on archival HST/ACS imaging of a single field $\sim 4^\prime$ from the galaxy centre (GO-15902). We detect 1441 RR Lyrae stars (1064 RRab, 363 RRc, and 14 of uncertain mode) and 35 anomalous Cepheids, and measure their periods, amplitudes, and intensity-mean magnitudes in the F606W and F814W bands. The variable population is dominated by RR Lyrae stars, as expected for a predominantly old (>10 Gyr) field with no strong young component. From the red giant branch tip we derive a distance modulus of $\mu = 24.68 \pm 0.06$ mag. The distribution of the RR Lyrae stars in the Bailey diagram, the fraction of RRc stars, and the presence of a substantial population of high-amplitude short-period RRab stars, indicate a range of metallicities extending to a metal-rich component, while the ratio of RR Lyrae stars to red giant branch stars indicates an extended star formation history, with only a modest fraction of the stellar mass formed in the first few Gyr. The anomalous Cepheids place NGC 205 among the slow evolvers on the relation between their frequency and host luminosity, and comparison with evolutionary models constrains their progenitors to $[\mathrm{Fe/H}] \lesssim -2.1$, indicating that metal-poor gas remained available well after the galaxy had begun to enrich. In a forthcoming paper, we will use the RR Lyrae periods and intensity-mean magnitudes to derive individual metallicities for these stars and trace the chemical enrichment history of NGC 205.

title: "Helium Enrichment Law": The Relation Between Helium and Metal Enrichment in Stars in FIRE-3 Simulations of Milky Way-mass Galaxies
comment: 17 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to ApJ
summary: Helium abundance is a key input to stellar models that are used to infer accurate ages, masses, and compositions for individually resolved stars in the Milky Way (MW), underpinning Galactic archaeology. Since spectroscopically measuring He abundances is difficult, stellar models often assume a fixed "chemical enrichment law" dY/dZ (the slope linearly relating a star's helium mass fraction Y to its metal mass fraction Z). If incorrect, this assumption can introduce significant systematics in inferring stellar properties. Using the FIRE-3 cosmological baryonic zoom-in simulations, we investigate helium versus metal enrichment in the stars of MW-mass galaxies. Given the nucleosynthetic yields in FIRE-3, overall metal production is dominated by core-collapse supernovae (CCSN) at all progenitor metallicities. He production is dominated by CCSN for progenitor metallicities of Z <= 0.1 Zsun, but by stellar winds for progenitors near Zsun. Our simulations produce a range of dY/dZ slopes slopes with best-fit values of ~0.75-2.1 depending on the age of the stars considered at present day; on average consistent with the range of values from MW observations but with no single "universal" enrichment law. The dY/dZ slope also shows galaxy-to-galaxy variance in our simulations, and to leading order increases over cosmic time within the same galaxy, based on the peculiarities of the formation histories of each MW-mass system. Despite choosing a fixed set of nucleosynthetic yields for stellar feedback processes in FIRE-3, we predict variance in dY/dZ for stars in MW-mass galaxies, and observations of MW stars must be interpreted in this context.

title: Little Red Dots with Broad H$β$ Lines Reveal the Black Hole Mass Function at 7<z<9.5
comment: 24 pages, 9 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to ApJ
summary: We present a systematic search for broad H$\beta$ emission at $7<z<9.5$ in 21,770 JWST/NIRSpec PRISM spectra drawn from four blank fields and six lensing clusters with photometry spanning 1942 arcmin$^2$. We find a sample of 20 sources with statistically significant broad-H$\beta$ emission, including 13 new sources. Our entire sample has colors and morphologies consistent with little red dots (LRDs), compared to only 37\% of broad-line emitters at $3.5<z<6$. Interpreting the broad-lines as indicators of Broad-line Active Galactic Nuclei (BLAGN), we infer black hole masses of $4.2\times10^{6}-2.1\times10^{8}$\,$M_{\odot}$. We calculate completeness corrections and construct the black hole mass function at $z\sim8$. The normalization of the black hole mass function rises by $\approx1.0$~dex from $z\sim8-5$, consistent with average black hole growth at $f_{\textrm{Edd}}\approx0.1$. Comparing with cosmological simulations, the $z\sim8$ black hole mass function requires heavy ($10^5$\,$M_{\odot}$) seeds or super-Eddington accretion onto light or intermediate mass seeds to match its normalization. Finally, we infer bolometric luminosities for the sample and construct a bolometric luminosity function. We integrate over this luminosity function to derive a black hole accretion density (BHAD) of $4.8^{+5.8}_{-2.6}\times10^{-7}~M_{\odot}~\textrm{yr}^{-1}~\textrm{Mpc}^{-3}$, showing broad agreement with previous photometric work, but disagreement with previous X-ray models, reinforcing the idea that BLAGN are more common in the early universe than previously expected.

title: The UKIRT M33 Monitoring Project - VII. A 15-year K-band photometric catalogue of long-period variable stars in the central kiloparsec of M33
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We present a homogenised K-band photometric catalogue for the central ${\approx}12$ arcmin$^2$ (${\approx}0.9$ kpc$^2$) of the Triangulum spiral galaxy M33, combining four independent PSF-based near-infrared datasets obtained with UKIRT between 2003 and 2018. These comprise the 2003-2007 UIST multi-epoch monitoring survey, the 2005 UFTI K-band mosaic (for which we present new PSF photometry), new WFCAM PSF reductions for the four central tiles, and a single K-band epoch from the 2018 UKIRT Hemisphere Survey (UHS DR3). Cross-matching all four catalogues and retaining stars detected in at least two of them yields 847 unique stars comprising 21,085 valid K-band measurements spanning a baseline of 15.11 yr. Photometric homogenisation onto the 2MASS/Vega system via 82 low-scatter calibration stars removes systematic inter-dataset offsets of up to 0.22 mag. Of the 847 monitored stars, 771 (91 per cent) are classified as variable ($\sigma_{\rm rms} > 0.10$ mag), including 385 high-amplitude variables ($A_K \geq 1.0$ mag): prime Mira-type long-period variable candidates for period determination. Cross-matching with archival Spitzer IRAC photometry yields 156 matched stars, of which 120 satisfy $\langle K\rangle - [3.6] > 0.5$ mag, identifying dust-enshrouded AGB candidates inaccessible to all-sky optical surveys. This catalogue constitutes the most extensive near-infrared photometric baseline assembled for AGB stars in any spiral galaxy beyond the Milky Way, providing the photometric foundation for the period-luminosity analysis and star-formation-history reconstruction in the companion Paper VIII. The full catalogue is available at the Centre de Données astronomiques de Strasbourg (CDS).

title: The Role of Star Formation and Morphology in the Mass-Metallicity Relation of Galaxies at Cosmic Noon
comment: Submitted to ApJ. Main text has 23 pages, including 10 figures. Comments welcome
summary: We investigate the dependence of the mass-metallicity relation (MZR) on star formation and galaxy morphology at 1.7<z<3.5, using JWST/NIRISS wide-field slitless spectroscopy of >1000 galaxies. The observations span >85 arcmin^2 from the pure-parallel PASSAGE and OutThere surveys. We derive gas-phase metallicities using a Bayesian framework that combines multiple strong emission-line ratios calibrated against direct auroral-line metallicity measurements from JWST. We constrain stellar masses, star formation rates (SFRs), and morphological properties using ancillary HST and JWST imaging. We stack spectra by stellar mass to constrain the MZR over log(M*/M)~6.5-11, and find that it is well described by a second-order polynomial, with a steep low-mass slope and metallicities<10% solar at log(M*/M)<7.5. Additional stacking by SFR and morphology reveals strong evidence for a fundamental metallicity relation (FMR). Specifically, at log(M*/M)<9.5, galaxies with lower SFRs are more metal-rich than those with higher SFRs at fixed mass. At log(M*/M)<9.5, we find that larger galaxies, and those having lower SFR surface densities, bulges, and/or spiral features are significantly metal rich relative to their smaller, higher SFR surface density, bulge-less, and/or non-spiral counterparts. These results suggest the secondary dependencies of the MZR reflect variations in the baryon cycle, such that recent metal-poor gas accretion drives concentrated star formation and metallicity dilution, while structurally developed galaxies retain more chemically enriched gas reservoirs.

title: Galactic Dynamics Drives Cyclic Star Formation in Dipole Dwarf Galaxies
comment: 27 pages, 12 figures
summary: Dwarf galaxies are dark matter-dominated systems that are sensitive to feedback and display bursty star formation histories. This makes them ideal probes of the processes that regulate star formation. This work investigates the timescales of star formation rate (SFR) variability in isolated dwarf galaxies using high-resolution cosmological zoom-in simulations of $50$ dwarf galaxies drawn from the Marvelous Massive Dwarfs and Extended Marvelous Dwarfs simulation suites ($7.3 <$ \lmstar $< 9.1$). We measure star formation histories in $10$ Myr bins and characterize their variability with power spectral densities (PSDs). At the population level, the PSDs of both disk and non-disk galaxies follow a broken power-law, with a break timescale near $100$ Myr. Individually, our galaxies show both smooth and bursty star formation. A subset of disk galaxies show quasi-periodic SFR oscillations about their mean, which we refer to as cyclic star formation. The dominant timescale of these oscillations scales linearly with half-light radius and is approximated by the orbital period at that radius. Cyclic galaxies have Magellanic Spiral (Sm) morphologies and host lopsided dipole gas disks. In these systems, the bulk of the gas in the lopsided disk moves between its maximum and minimum distance from the galactic center, compressing the star-forming gas once per radial orbit and driving the SFR cycle. Cyclic star formation adds a narrow Lorentzian component to the PSD, peaked at radial orbital frequency of the disk ($\sim 200-500$ Myr), which is comparable to burst timescales inferred from observations.

title: What shapes the bright end of the UV luminosity function? Stellar mass, star-formation variability, and dust in JADES
comment: 39 pages, 25 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to MNRAS. Comments welcome. Machine-readable tables: doi: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23697784
summary: JWST surveys find more UV-bright galaxies at $z>10$ than galaxy-formation models predict, but the roles of recent star formation, stellar mass and dust remain uncertain. We analyse 1365 spectroscopically confirmed JADES galaxies at $3\leq z\leq9$, fitting NIRCam photometry and NIRSpec emission lines with \ceri. Our model includes flexible star-formation histories (SFHs) under three priors, two-component dust attenuation and nebular emission. We account for spectroscopic selection through population reweighting and assess the reliability of inferred trends. At $z=3$--5, rising SFHs are more common in low-mass galaxies, whereas most galaxies above $10^{9.5}\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$ have declining SFHs. The apparent increase in rising fractions with redshift cannot be distinguished from the adopted SFH prior alone. At fixed stellar mass, recent star formation is the strongest predictor of UV brightness. UV-brighter galaxies have higher recent SFRs, younger stellar populations and less attenuation at fixed SFR. Below $10^9\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$, they are also more likely to have rising SFHs, with odds increasing by up to a factor of 2.3 per magnitude brighter, although the strongest trend requires caution. In contrast, galaxies with $M_{\mathrm{UV}}<-20$ at $z=3$--5 are predominantly massive, and approximately half have declining SFHs. Dust partly offsets burst-driven UV brightening: attenuation increases with recent SFR and declines gradually after the inferred SFR peak. In model sensitivity tests, dust has the largest effect on bright-end counts, whereas removing galaxy-to-galaxy SFH scatter changes them by at most 0.17~dex. Thus, bursts can make low-mass galaxies unusually UV-bright for their mass, while the absolute bright end of the UVLF is primarily shaped by stellar mass and dust attenuation.

title: Measuring the magnetization profiles of galaxy groups and clusters
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures
summary: Magnetic fields are vital in determining the physical conditions of baryons in massive halos. They are, however, notoriously difficult to observe. This impacts problems from our understanding of galaxy formation, to the observed deficit in the amplitude of thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) power spectrum that affects cosmological inferences. Although Faraday rotation measures (RMs) offer a direct probe of magnetic fields, it weights magnetic fields by the free-electron density. Several probes of free electrons, including fast radio burst (FRB) dispersion measures (DMs) and kinematic SZ (kSZ) effect, are now maturing into precision tools. We combine RM$^2$ stacks from SPICE-RACS around DESI galaxy groups and ROSAT clusters with optical depth profiles constrained jointly by the FRB DM-redshift relation and the kSZ effect, and obtain 95% upper limits on the rms line-of-sight magnetic field of $<3.9$-$11.6~\mu$G ($<2.3$-$6.4~\mu$G) in groups (clusters) for a 10~kpc coherence length. Combining these with thermal pressure profiles inferred from tSZ-shear cross-correlations, we obtain 95% lower limits on the plasma $\beta$ of $>0.31$ ($>11$) in groups (clusters). Although current constraints are only limits, we forecast a first detection with larger datasets from the Deep Synoptic Array (DSA). We present the first forecast of the DSA RM grid density ($\sim365$ RMs deg$^{-2}$), which when combined with 10$^4$ FRBs would measure the field in groups to $3$-$13\%$ precision, compared to current constraints of $38$-$75\%$. Although the interpretation of current measurements remains challenging owing to depolarization along turbulent halo sightlines and the unknown coherence length, larger samples and DSA/Square Kilometer Array observations may resolve these uncertainties by measuring polarization-fraction profiles and the RM structure function using extended radio sources, respectively.

title: The Spatially-Resolved Recent Star Formation History of the M81 Disk
comment: 24 pages, 13 figures, 2 tables; Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: The nearby M81 galaxy---a tidally interacting $L^*$ spiral disk---offers a unique perspective on the interplay of secular and external processes in shaping galaxy properties. We present the most detailed, panoramic map of M81's stellar populations to date, using archival Hubble Space Telescope ACS photometry from the ANGST survey spanning the full optical extent of its disk. From color-magnitude diagram fitting, we recover spatially-resolved star formation histories (SFHs) over the last $\sim180\,$Myr. M81's global SFH is remarkably steady in the last $\sim180\,$Myr with slight enhancements seen $\lesssim15\,$Myr ago. The average SFR surface density rises toward the center before falling off within the innermost $\sim4\,$kpc. The disk is also notably lopsided, with the eastern half having formed $\sim50\%$ more stars than the western half over the same area---a trend missed by FUV-based SFR indicators due to dust systematics. Finally, the long-term SFHs of both M81 and M82 point to a pericenter passage $\sim1\,$Gyr ago. By identifying M81-M82 analogs in the TNG50 cosmological simulation, we rule out the more recent pericenter times of $150-220\,$Myr predicted by some works, as such passages are inconsistent with M81's undisturbed SFH over the last $\sim180\,$Myr. With this work, M81 becomes only the third $L^*$ spiral---after M31 and NGC 6946---to have its SFH spatially resolved across large areas of its disk.

title: The SIRMOS mission concept: a space-based near-IR spectroscopic survey of 100 million galaxies in the Euclid Wide Survey footprint
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures, 6 tables, presented at SPIE Space Telescopes and Instrumentation 2026: Optical, Infrared, and Millimeter Wave (August 2026)
summary: SIRMOS is a mission concept for a future NASA Astrophysics Explorer opportunity that aims to revolutionize our understanding of the universe by mapping the large-scale structure of galaxies in unprecedented breadth and detail to explore cosmic origins and evolution. Specifically, the primary science goals of SIRMOS are to discover how cosmic inflation seeded large-scale structure, reveal the nature of the accelerating expansion of the universe, and measure the sum of neutrino masses to exceptionally high precision. Its secondary science goals include determining how environment shapes galaxy evolution at cosmic noon and beyond, and probing the Milky Way's dust-enshrouded regions, reaching the far side of our Galaxy. To accomplish its transformative science goals, SIRMOS executes a 3-year cosmology survey over the Euclid footprint of ~14,000 deg$^2$, obtaining slit spectra for ~100 million galaxies at 1<z<4. SIRMOS is the first space mission designed specifically to leverage Euclid's wide near-infrared (IR) imaging survey for target selection and employs a digital micro-mirror device (DMD) to acquire up to 4,000 simultaneous spectra over a wide 0.9 deg$^2$ field of view. The instrument's excellent spectral resolution of $R=1300$ and continuous wavelength coverage from 1.25--2.5 $\mu$m capture the redshifts of distant galaxies with no gaps, reducing systematic biases to achieve ground-breaking science.
